story_text.value:
Hey HN!

It's Ved, the founder of Merget.

Merget is a GitHub App that connects to your code repositories and autonomously manages your PR queue using deep static analysis.

We can detect overlapping semantic relationships, order your queue in the most optimal order, and resolve merge conflicts in parallel across all of your PRs, ensuring your tests and CI continue to pass.

In short, you can advance main by dozens of PRs with a single click, safely :)

We hope to ease the burden of code produced by agentic workloads and save dev teams time and tokens! It's free to try.

title.value: Show HN: Merget – Merge queue using code graphs to order and resolve GitHub PRs

story_text.value:
I run a small school for gifted kids in Honolulu, and our students do some of their math practice on iPads. I wanted a 9-year-old to be able to type 3 2/5 the way she'd write it on paper, and couldn't find a React Native component that did it. MathLive and MathQuill are good editors, but they're built on the DOM, so in React Native they only run inside a WebView, and I didn't want a WebView inside every answer box.

It's harder than you might think to to make sure arrow keys, taps in parentheses, delete keys, tab key, etc. on a hardware keyboard all work as expected. We packaged it up so other schools/builders don't need to reinvent the wheel.

It's drawn with react-native-svg and runs in Expo Go. A dev build adds two small iOS modules.

We pulled it out of the tutoring app our students use every day and put it under MIT. It hasn't been run on Android yet. Web support is new in 0.1.1: 0.1.0 crashed on react-native-web, which I found out while taking a screenshot for this post.

title.value: Show HN: A React Native math keypad for kids – fractions, exponents, no WebView

story_text.value:
This is a fast typing word puzzle game meant to make you think about what words might not ever have been written (or said) in some long or famous texts. You can combine texts for a harder challenge, and when you're done you can send your results and the link to your friends if you'd like.

I'm the type of guy who has a ton of projects all "in development" at the same time, so in 2026 I'm doing my best to actually finish and launch a few. The idea for this game came to me fully formed yesterday and threw off my momentum with other stuff, but I figured I might be able to publish it within a day. For anyone else struggling with this problem, I strongly recommend trying to publish a quick idea as fast as you can.

This is the first time I've shared anything on Show HN. I'm really interested in not publishing slop games, so I spent a long time, proportional to the rest of the development, on the UX. If it's slop, let me know!

story_text.value:
Hi HN. I have potato computer. I tried running this flash game (N, the way of the ninja!) from 2004 (!), but my laptop from 2016 struggled to run it (yes, even with official Flashplayer!).

I don't know what gives, but I know it wasn't that slow back in the day! But I know ActionScript and JS are basically the same language, and that a WebGL shim for the Flash graphics API can't be that hard... so I asked DeepSeek to give it a stab, and $2 later I can play the game at normal frame rate :)

This falls under various kinds of infringement I imagine, but also it's >20 year old abandonware (and free marketing for Metanet -- hi! :) so... yeah...

Please enjoy.

p.s. I also added controller support. Not configurable yet but should work ok out of the box.

---

EDIT: Just found that the official version is up here, using Ruffle (though it lags unplayable on my device):

https://www.thewayoftheninja.org/nv2.html

Ruffle version has better graphics though. Ninja ended up a bit anemic in the port!

story_text.value:
Hi all,

Recently, Opus 5.5 and I as lowly Director in Chief (but I still feel like I matter, and that I'm good enough and smart enough to be involved, doggone it!), revamped this LR clone with procedural levels/music (it already had that, this was just a broad improvement/enhancement pass). It was ok'ish before but after the overhaul I was kind of taken back with how playable and good it is now.

Added multiplayer and playing on a TV (Android/Google TV app and should work with a paired BT controller).

It's pretty fun I have to say. I get bored with most LR's after a bit but this one I actually want to keep playing. It's unique (I think) with the seeded procedural unlimited levels and procedural synth music, and also you can choose Soma Space Station streaming radio for the music which usually fits in perfectly. And it has some added touches like a piece of red outlined gold that you cannot reach and can only get from an AI whose captured it etc, and you can change the difficulty to pretty insane levels. Normal mode is already challenging.

A little tech/stack info: All game rules are now implemented using a TypeScript simulation environment that is separate from Phaser. This allows use of the exact same logic to render the game, run tests against the game, and verify that the levels created by the level generation system are valid and complete enough. The level creation process uses a solver to analyze possible movements and digging actions that a player could take, and verifies that a level can actually be completed.

Built w TypeScript, Phaser 4, and Vite (client), Go server that handles the web app and the TV/phone-controller connection.

I think it's performant enough, but not sure if the stack/architecture could be rethought to make it faster and lighter and less potential lag on lower end devices etc. This is basically vibe-coded, I'm more a Linux/ops guy than a developer or programmer.

Feedback welcomed.

https://loderunner2099.exe.xyz https://loderunner2099.exe.xyz/tv https://loderunner2099.exe.xyz/app https://loderunner2099.exe.xyz/pad

story_text.value:
Budget is a free, open-source app for Mac and Windows. With the simple mode, it gives you what you'd expect of a budgeting app: configure budgets and track expenses against those budgets. But, if you're a geek like me and are way too interested in your personal finance, the extended mode offers features like carrying leftover budgets to the next month, splitting expenses across multiple budgets and seeing how much you can freely spend the coming year, while taking into account any large future expenses (like a car insurance where the premium is paid on a yearly basis).

This app is the result of a hobby of mine to track my expenses. It started a few years ago in a spreadsheet, but that spreadsheet at some point took me minutes to edit on my MacBook with 8 gigs of RAM. I had the idea to turn it into an app before, but never had the time to do so.

I worked in the software industry until halfway through 2024, when LLMs were mostly just used for debugging. But, because of all the positivity I heard about how good they've gotten now, I tried to see if I could turn the spreadsheet into an app with the help of Claude Opus 5.5. I had to point out a couple of bugs and bad decisions (like bad alignment of text and using entire English sentences instead of keywords as keys for translation), but overall, it worked really well.

Budgeting apps are of course not new. But, they often are either free but with limited features, free but with an obnoxious amount of cookies and/or ads, free but charge money for important features or charge money to be used at all. The idea of this project is that there are no cookies, no ads, no fees, no data being stored remotely and that the code is open-source. Data ownership stands at the center of the app: you can easily export/import your data and create back-ups (besides the automatic back-ups the app creates for you). It is available to everyone, of course as long as you have a device that is supported (currently only devices that run macOS and Windows).

I'm interested to hear if you think this app has any potential and if you think any important features are missing.

title.value: Show HN: Budget – an open-source private budgeting app for Mac and Windows

story_text.value:
Long story short, I needed a way to enable/disable skills for specific projects, but for how nice Claude CLI is, it kinda sucks in this regard.

I wanted it to do 2-3 things well, be fast, and not bloat it. Of course, I then prompted it into existence.

Features: - Shows the available settings for your specific Claude version (always in sync). - Configure CLAUDE.md, settings.json, Skills, Plugins and MCPs. - Tree-view in the sidebar to view all Claude projects. - Gives useful suggestions for enabling privacy-related settings.

It's a single Go binary for macOS, Linux and Windows, MIT licensed.

You can find a screenshot and more info here: https://github.com/claude-settings-xyz/claudia

Curious what you think (and how it's so bad and vibecoded).

---

If you like such tools, these 2 might be helpful: - CODEXED — The same thing but for Codex CLI (https://github.com/codex-config/codexed) - SWITCHEROO — Switch local CLI accounts for 10+ providers (Wrangler, Vercel, Claude, Github etc) (https://github.com/FTCHD/switcheroo)

story_text.value:
Hi HN, I'm Frank, founder of Truce.

Truce is a neutral AI mediator. Each side tells it their side in private, Truce proposes one specific outcome, and nothing happens unless both people sign.

The part that may interest you is the agent side. Truce is a remote MCP server (https://trucehq.com/mcp) with 12 tools, so an assistant can start a Truce for its user, or answer one for the other person with their consent.

There is also "Agent Truce": two agents acting for different people or companies settle a dispute between themselves, such as a refund, a late delivery or an invoice. Each agent gives its side, its evidence and a private mandate from its human, for example "may pay up to $300". The mediator never sees either mandate, so it proposes on the merits. A proposal that fits inside both mandates is accepted automatically; anything else goes back to the humans. Truce never moves money.

It's free for AI agents. One-minute demo on the page.

I'd especially like criticism of the mandate design. How would you game it, and what would make you trust it for your own agents?

story_text.value:
Two years ago, I tried making a sudoku game in React, but I let it go because getting everything properly implemented turned out to be quite a bit of work. Then AI came along. I’ve spent the past few weeks working hard on Klink in the evenings and on weekends.

It started out with experimenting a Tamagotchi-style game where you had to take care of a little robot and gradually add more parts to it. But it turned out that a Tamagotchi on an iPhone didn’t really work, I was just mashing buttons and it didn't give me that same feeling I got as a kid clicking the little buttons to feed my pixelated friend. I then thought of a talk given by Theo (the T3 Youtuber) about how we should all think bigger when working with AI and I’ve always wanted to make a sudoku game. So that got me thinking about the sudoku games/apps I played in the past.

I’ve always found sudoku games a bit dry. Other than a "Daily Challenge" there isn't really an incentive to have me coming back and then after a few days I forget all about it. So I started with prompting and kept prompting and prompting until I’d built a sudoku app that was actually usable, with one extra mechanic: building and upgrading a little robot. The flow of the game is that you solve a puzzle, this gives you scrap, that scrap is then used to "buy" new components, or upgrade existing components. (each component has Mk I, Mk II, Mk III versions)

I'm Dutch and it's Sinterklaas season here, so I added an in-game event where you can earn robot parts themed around the holiday. They're only available during this time of the year. Up next will probably be Christmas.

Alongside classic sudoku, I added quite a few variants (Killer, Thermo, Sandwich, Arrows, Diagonal, Chaos (Jigsaw), Kropki, Even/Odd, Hyper, Binaro, and Trees and Tents). I also added “Tricks,” which are basically short lessons on how to use standard sudoku techniques and recognize patterns. Then I polished the app a bit more and finally released it to the App Store last Friday. You can play it on iOS, iPadOS, and macOS.

Since Friday, I’ve had a whopping 15 downloads, mostly from friends and family (to be honest, probably all of them). I also made a website: https://klinksudoku.com. Normally I just work as a developer at a company and this is my first time I actually have to think about things like marketing, getting more users, promoting the product which is very fun to experience.

Currently I’m also looking for Android testers. Since I have a personal developer account, Google requires me to have 12 people in a closed test before I can release the app publicly. You can join the test group here: https://groups.google.com/g/klink-sudoku-testers

I’m curious what you think.

title.value: Show HN: Klink – I built a sudoku game where every puzzle helps rebuild a robot

Alongside classic sudoku, I added quite a few variants (Killer, Thermo, Sandwich, Arrows, Diagonal, Chaos (Jigsaw), Kropki, Even/Odd, Hyper, Binaro, and Trees and Tents). I also added “Tricks,” which are basically short lessons on how to use standard sudoku techniques and recognize patterns. Then I polished the app a bit more and finally released it to the App Store last Friday. You can play it on iOS, iPadOS, and macOS.

Since Friday, I’ve had a whopping 15 downloads, mostly from friends and family (to be honest, probably all of them). I also made a website: https://klinksudoku.com. Normally I just work as a developer at a company and this is my first time I actually have to think about things like marketing, getting more users, promoting the product which is very fun to experience.

Currently I’m also looking for Android testers. Since I have a personal developer account, Google requires me to have 12 people in a closed test before I can release the app publicly. You can join the test group here: https://groups.google.com/g/klink-sudoku-testers

I’m curious what you think.
